segments.voice: Yesterday we left the Rudram where it lives, chanted while water pours over the stone, the fierce one met with a bow. Your line was the Rudram. What did you pour on yesterday? Now the night. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.
screen: `THE RUDRAM, POURED OVER STONE.` · `NOW THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Diwali fills a night with lamps. Holi fills a morning with color. Maha Shivaratri asks for something stranger. Don't eat. Don't sleep. Stay up in the dark, through the hours when the house goes quiet and the street goes still, and keep your attention on one thing until the sky starts to gray. There is no finale of fireworks. The reward, if there is one, comes at dawn, to someone who is tired and hungry and still there. You've met this night before on the path, through its stories: the hunter in the tree, the pillar of fire. This week is different. We take the night itself, hour by hour, as a course of study. Today, just the shape of it.
screen: `DON'T EAT. DON'T SLEEP.` → `ATTENTION ON ONE THING TILL DAWN.` → `THE NIGHT ITSELF, AS A COURSE.`

segments.voice: The name says it plainly. Maha, great. Shiva. Ratri, night. The great night of Shiva. Tradition places it in the dark half of the lunar month, on the night just before the new moon, when there is almost no moon left to see by. The Shiva Purana describes a vow for this night. Fast through the day. Worship Shiva in the linga, with water and bilva leaves. And stay awake until morning. That's the whole syllabus, and it's short enough to fit on a card. But notice what kind of teaching it is. Nobody hands you a book. Nobody gives a lecture. The night teaches through the body. Hunger is one lesson. Sleepiness is another. The dark is a third. Each one takes away something you usually lean on, food, rest, light, and then asks what's left to lean on instead. Some readers hear the near-moonless sky that way too: the mind with its usual light gone, and only one thing worth turning toward. So this week we'll go through the night in order, the way a student goes through a course. The vow made in the morning. The fast. Keeping awake. The name repeated through the dark. The offerings. And finally dawn, and what you do with it. One piece a day. Some people keep every hour of this night, in a temple crowded until sunrise. Some keep a part of it at home. Some only learn about it. The course is the same either way. Its first lesson fits in a sentence: the night is not an empty space between two days. On this night, the night is the point.
screen: `MAHA, SHIVA, RATRI.` · `FAST, WORSHIP, STAY AWAKE.` · `THE NIGHT TEACHES THROUGH THE BODY.` · `ONE PIECE OF THE NIGHT A DAY.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small dark. If you can, dim the light around you, or simply close your eyes. Settle, and let the breath slow. Notice what the dark takes away: the screen, the faces, the things to look at. Then notice what it gives back. Sounds you hadn't heard. The weight of your body. The breath, which was there all along. Keep your attention on one thing, the breath is enough, and come back to it whenever you drift. If you pray, you can hold Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as that one thing. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, taken this week as a night curriculum. Today, its shape: a fast, worship, and staying awake until dawn.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Tonight, before you sleep, spend one minute in the dark on purpose, and notice what it gives back. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep it may fast, visit Shiva temples or worship at home, offer water, milk and bilva leaves to the linga, and stay awake through the night with chanting and singing.

notes: First of seven Shivaratri days (1153–1159). Plan for the week, one piece of the night per day: shape (1153), the vow/sankalpa (1154), the fast (1155, week end), keeping awake (1156), the name through the night (1157), the offerings (1158), dawn and breaking the fast (1159, close of the Shiva part). The hunter and the pillar of fire were told in years 1–4 already, so they are only named here.
The index word is cut off ('Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum'); kept exactly as required. Suggest the outline give this run a proper word (e.g. 'Maha Shivaratri' or 'jagarana').

Calendar: Maha Shivaratri falls on the chaturdashi of the krishna paksha (Magha by the amanta reckoning, Phalguna by the purnimanta). Stated only as 'the dark half of the lunar month, the night just before the new moon', attributed to tradition; confirm.
Confirm the Shiva Purana location of the Shivaratri vrata (Koti Rudra Samhita; also Vidyeshvara Samhita) and that fasting, linga worship with bilva and water, and keeping awake are all in it.
'Some readers' reading of the near-moonless night as the mind without its usual light is offered as interpretation, not doctrine.
Editor pass: fixed one ungrammatical line in the hook ('There's no fireworks finale'); otherwise unchanged.
